notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Very mountainous with fjords along most of the coast. Finland and Denmark are mostly flat; Sweden is mixed.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Long white plates with the blue EU strip; vans and commercial vehicles have green plates, most commonly seen in this country.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Small roads have long dashed white edge lines; bigger roads have solid edge lines and a yellow centre line with an orange tinge.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Road lines are often built up from small dots of paint.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Thin, curved rectangular bollards with the reflector inside a black parallelogram.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Orange snow poles with a fairly thin white reflector near the middle; Sweden's reflector is wider and higher, Finland's is at the very top.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Thin wooden snow poles with painted reflectors are fairly common; elsewhere in the north they usually lack reflectors.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Wooden utility poles, often with a small black metal cap on top; lamps are fixed with a single thick bolt, not the double bolting used in Sweden and Finland.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: Guardrails often have wooden posts, which is uncommon in Sweden or Finland.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Traffic signs have a red outline on a white background; Swedish and Finnish ones are yellow.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Direction signs are yellow with a black border; road numbers sit in a green box for major roads and a white box for smaller ones.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Chevrons are yellow on black.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Small roads often have blue signs with a big white M; Sweden's font differs, and Finland has none.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Pedestrian sign usually has four stripes and a very simple figure; variants have five stripes or a detailed figure wearing a hat.

notes.subject: street
notes.text: Bus stops usually have a small blue sign with a white bus.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: White signs reading "Sone", usually with a speed limit, are common in towns.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Small white square signs show the road number and the distance to the nearest town; numbers start with R or F.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Street names end in -veien, -gata or -gate, attached to the name. Swedish uses väg and a detached gata; Danish uses vej and gade.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Special letters Æ, Ø and Å. Danish has all three, Swedish only Å, and Icelandic has Æ.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Mostly wooden houses, often red, with many black ones and more white ones than in Sweden or Finland. Traditional homes may have grass roofs.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: The first digit of road numbers depends on the region, with some exceptions among one- and two-digit roads.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Bilingual signs with a Sámi language appear in the north; look for Á, Đ and runs of several vowels.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Russian sometimes appears on signs near the eastern border, mostly on the E6 and E105 near Kirkenes.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The biggest farmland area, flatter than most of the country, with rolling land and smooth forested hills in the distance.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Farmland around the central fjord city is very hilly, with steeper, more uneven hills than the southeast.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Flat, vast open grass fields with walls of large round rocks, south of Stavanger.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Deep fjords ringed by tall mountains are most common between Bergen and Trondheim; black snow poles also cluster there.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Sharp, rocky, nearly treeless mountains on the northern island chain.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Rolling land rather than tall mountains, with tiny birches and patchy grass.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Barren highlands with no trees or bushes and rocky mountains alongside the road.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Whole villages of white wooden houses on the southern coast, where bare rock with small coastal pines is common.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Small, wide black pole plates with a single line of letters and digits in the southeast.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: Rusty guardrails almost only on the coast, especially the southern half of the west coast.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: An old mining town in the east-central mountains has dense traditional wooden architecture.
